clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous variants or 17q12 microdeletions affecting HNF1B, a transcription factor governing development of the kidney, pancreas, liver and genital tract
The renal phenotype is highly variable, most often bilateral renal cysts or hyperechoic kidneys detected antenatally or in childhood, but also hypoplasia, dysplasia and single kidney
The classic association is renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD): a maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY5) coupled with structural kidney disease
Extrarenal features include pancreatic hypoplasia with exocrine insufficiency, abnormal liver enzymes, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia and genital tract anomalies (for example a bicornuate uterus)
Hypomagnesaemia from renal magnesium wasting is a useful biochemical clue
A large proportion of cases arise de novo, so absence of family history does not exclude the diagnosis
Diagnosis requires genetic testing including deletion analysis, because a whole-gene deletion is a common mechanism
reference.pathophysiology: HNF1B (hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-beta) is a transcription factor essential for the normal development and differentiation of the kidney, pancreatic islet and exocrine tissue, biliary tract and Mullerian structures. Loss of one functional copy, through point variants or a 17q12 contiguous gene deletion, causes haploinsufficiency that disrupts nephrogenesis and tubular gene expression, producing cystic, hypoplastic or dysplastic kidneys and impaired tubular handling of magnesium and urate. The same developmental defect in the pancreas leads to beta-cell dysfunction and diabetes (MODY5) with exocrine hypoplasia, and in the genital tract to Mullerian anomalies. The resulting phenotype is therefore a multisystem developmental disorder with prominent structural and functional kidney disease.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (other genes)
Multicystic dysplastic kidney and other CAKUT
Other MODY subtypes and type 2 diabetes
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound to characterise cysts, echogenicity, size and structural anomalies
Serum magnesium and urate (renal wasting patterns support the diagnosis)
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to detect diabetes
Liver function tests and pancreatic imaging where indicated
Pelvic imaging for genital tract anomalies in females
Genetic testing of HNF1B including copy-number analysis for the 17q12 deletion
redFlags: Antenatally detected bilateral hyperechoic or cystic kidneys
New-onset diabetes with structural kidney disease in a young non-obese patient
Progressive decline in renal function towards kidney failure
Neurodevelopmental features suggesting a larger 17q12 deletion
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable, ranging from stable mild renal impairment to progression to kidney failure; the combination of diabetes, electrolyte disturbance and structural anomalies requires lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because sequencing is normal without testing for a whole-gene deletion
Overlooking hypomagnesaemia as a diagnostic clue
Assuming diabetes is type 1 or type 2 and missing the MODY5 label affecting management
Failing to consider de novo cases in the absence of family history
references: GeneReviews / OMIM entries on HNF1B-related disease
management: Manage the associated MODY5 diabetes, usually with insulin as sulphonylureas are less effective given the developmental beta-cell defect and coexisting exocrine insufficiency
Replace magnesium orally for symptomatic renal magnesium wasting and treat hyperuricaemia or gout with urate-lowering therapy
Institute chronic kidney disease care with blood-pressure control using renin-angiotensin blockade to slow progression
Screen for and manage extrarenal features, including pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with pancreatic enzyme replacement, deranged liver enzymes and genital tract anomalies
Monitor renal function, magnesium, urate, glycaemic control and imaging surveillance of cysts and structural anomalies
Plan kidney replacement therapy with dialysis or transplantation when progressing to kidney failure

Refer to clinical genetics for confirmatory HNF1B testing including 17q12 deletion analysis, with genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance and frequent de novo cases
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across nephrology, diabetes, gastroenterology and gynaecology
